Our mission

Building a truly human-like brain, in hardware.

Today's AI emulates intelligence on von Neumann hardware, run from distant data centres and reached over the internet. SkyNet, our Skyrmion Network, is different by design: it computes in the three-dimensional dynamics of topologically protected magnetic states, with memory and compute in the same place, on the device itself.

The problem

AI runs on an architecture designed for calculators

Today's AI emulates intelligence on the von Neumann design, where memory and compute sit apart and every operation shuttles data between them. Neuromorphic chips merge the two, as a brain does, and could run language and movement locally at brain-like power. The building blocks have been shown in academic labs. Getting them out of the lab is the hard part.

For a robot maker, the cost is carried on board

A robot carries its brain with it. Every watt spent on compute is a watt taken from the motors and the battery, and sending decisions to a data centre adds a round trip a moving robot cannot wait for. Today's robots mostly run models trained elsewhere, on chips that do not learn on the job.

Ground truth is rationed

The measurements that reveal 3D magnetic states sit at a handful of large national facilities. Time is allocated through competitive proposals, comparable beamlines are oversubscribed two to two-and-a-half times, and only around a tenth of beamtime is open to industry at all.

Even the nominally free academic route carries a hidden cost: months of proposal writing and peer review, sample preparation, travel and queueing, in exchange for a handful of shifts. Annual maintenance shutdowns shrink supply further, while the fields that most need these measurements, from spintronics and topological magnetism to neuromorphic and quantum devices, have grown far faster than capacity.

Magnetic memory leaders apply up to a year in advance. For anyone iterating on a new device, a few shifts twice a year is incompatible with a fast R&D loop, and there is no substitute technique to route the demand to. It isn't a market that's served. It's rationed.

The solution

Write, read and train, on our own ground-truth data

Computation should be embodied directly in the three-dimensional dynamics of topologically protected states of matter, not emulated on flat hardware. Writing to these devices already scales with photonics. Reading them doesn't, and without a reliable readout there is no way to train them. TopSpin is founded on three components that close that gap.

Component 1 · Write

SkyNet: topological 3D neuromorphic architectures

Skyrmions are tiny, topologically protected magnetic whirls, naturally able to store and process information in the same place. Existing proposals treat them as flat objects in a single plane. SkyNet treats depth as genuine computational bandwidth, so the third dimension does real work.

Component 2 · Read

LayerSight™: our proprietary readout

Any model of complex 3D magnetic structures has to be checked against real measurement. LayerSight separates the spin and orbital contributions to magnetism layer by layer, at nanometre depth and with ultrafast timing. It runs in our own lab, which removes the facilities bottleneck.

Component 3 · Train

An automated workflow from observing to training

A shortage of data has kept spintronics focused on observation. We combine advances in photonic computing, machine learning and materials discovery to write, read and train in one loop, opening the door to backpropagation-style training for physical hardware. The system improves with every experiment.

What customers get

On-board intelligence that learns, at brain-like power

Learns on the device

The chip's physical configuration is its trained state, so learning lives in the material, not in a distant data centre.

Brain-like power

Memory and compute sit in the same place, so no energy is spent shuttling data between them. The design target is power comparable to the human brain.

Interpretable by design

Each layer is read on its own, so a robot maker can see what the chip has learned, not just what it outputs.

How SkyNet learns

Conventional chips store a model's weights in memory and fetch them for every calculation. SkyNet holds them as the physical arrangement of the device itself.

Pseudo-stable states

A small, targeted nudge moves a skyrmion into a different but equally stable arrangement, and it stays there instead of relaxing back.

A physical weight set

Training sets the device's configuration layer by layer before inference begins, the hardware analogue of a trained set of weights.

The model picks the method

We are deliberately agnostic about how training is applied. Our AI model selects and refines the most viable mechanism rather than committing too early.

Computing by resonance

Once trained, the device is gently driven and its response does the computing, without disturbing what it has learned.

Read with light

The response is read optically rather than electrically, giving a rich, high-dimensional output instead of a handful of signals.

A light final step

A small, simple model turns that output into answers, so most of the work happens in the physics.

These are design targets. Power and task performance will be measured on hardware.

LayerSight™

The readout that makes SkyNet trainable

LayerSight reconstructs the neuromorphic dynamics layer by layer, at the spatial and temporal resolution training requires. The measurements it builds on have been confined to large national facilities. We have designed a benchtop instrument instead, so the whole development cycle stays in our own lab.

Why it hasn't been done: reading 3D chips at scale has been the field's open problem

The industry

Chips can be written and read one at a time, but not trained at scale: you can't backpropagate through a 3D state you can't see.

The state was never unseeable, only unmeasured. Ground-truth data was locked in synchrotrons, with measurements years apart.

Academia

Set 3D readout aside, and spun out devices with no route to read or train them at scale.

Reading the 3D state is possible: the depth-resolved technique behind LayerSight is published. It needed a readout built for the lab.

R&D scientists

Treated observation as the end goal, because no lab could generate training-scale datasets.

LayerSight makes training the goal, with data at the cadence machine learning needs.

The field isn't short of devices. It's missing a way to connect, read and train them.

That's what TopSpin builds. It's time to build neuromorphic computers properly.

Traction

What is de-risked, and what remains to be proven

De-risked so far

  • The core measurement is publishedThe depth-resolved technique LayerSight builds on, X-ray reflectometry ferromagnetic resonance, is published in Physical Review Letters (2020).
  • Instrument and chip designedConcept designs are complete for the benchtop LayerSight instrument and for SkyNet's optical readout chip and its carrier board.
  • The gap is mappedA systematic review of the skyrmion literature found no published measurement of layer-resolved skyrmion dynamics, and no experiment using separate layers of one stack as separate computing layers.

Still to prove

  • LayerSight matches the synchrotronBenchtop results agree with national-facility measurements on matched samples. Pre-seed, months 0–9.
  • Layers act independentlySeparate skyrmion populations in one stack can be written and read layer by layer. Pre-seed, months 9–24.
  • Trained states holdTrained configurations stay stable while the device computes.
  • Performance on hardwareTask accuracy and power, measured on a fabricated SkyNet device.
  • A route to volumeA foundry route for the magnetic stack and the readout chip, ahead of pilot fleets.

Commercial: partner outreach is funded by this round. We will approach ~30 robotics and edge-AI companies, aiming to sign 3 design partners by month 12.

Competition

Others fabricate every element in place, so their networks can't reshape themselves

Conventional neuromorphic chips wire up every neuron and synapse at the fab. Skyrmions form in the film on their own, and SkyNet uses depth as an extra dimension. The closest effort, the EU's SkyANN project, pursues skyrmion neural networks in a flat film.

Our founding protocol

A measurement-first design loop that ties hardware, measurement and machine learning together from day one, and closes before the architecture is finalised.

  1. Build

    A benchtop instrument with the resolution needed to see inside the device.

  2. Verify

    Check it against national-facility measurements on matched samples before trusting it as a training source.

  3. Train

    Teach an AI model on our measurements and established theory, working with materials discovery partners.

  4. Select

    Let the trained model finalise the SkyNet design and choose how to train it.

Month 24

De-risked: a validated benchtop instrument, a proprietary 3D spin dataset, a model-selected SkyNet stack to fabricate at seed, and Language AI and robotics collaborators.
